progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From B12: sequencing reads base order, profiling compares selected markers; sequencing thousands of people gives an allele's frequency. From B11: allele frequency = copies / all copies; a SNP is a one-base difference; association is not cause; sample size and representation limit conclusions. From B9: unaffected parents with an affected child show a recessive trait; carriers. From B7: the sickle allele is one base change in the haemoglobin gene; sickle-shaped red cells. Year 11 (Biological Diversity): natural selection removes alleles that lower survival or reproduction. Not assumed: large-scale collaborative project, inference, heterozygote advantage, genetic diversity as a population measure, founder, reference genome.
progression.startsWith: The hook: UK Biobank is a shared research project that began recruiting in 2006. Half a million volunteers in Britain, aged 40 to 69, gave blood samples and agreed to link their health records.
progression.stopsAfter: saying what a large-scale collaborative project is (many researchers and sites pooling data); explaining why a large sample detects a small effect that chance hides in a small one, giving stronger inference but not certainty; describing how pooled frequency data revealed the sickle allele as unexpectedly common; naming the three evidence streams (pedigree, DNA, frequency) and why their agreement matters; explaining heterozygote advantage with malaria; giving two reasons a matching pattern is not proof (coincidence; founders and chance in a small group); explaining how diversity data guide conservation and why diversity does not guarantee survival; explaining how shared variants indicate more recent common ancestry and what the 1000 Genomes pattern suggests; saying the reference genome is a composite, not everyone's genome; stating what large data improve and what they do not remove; applying this to unseen frequency and diversity data.
progression.nextLesson: what population patterns can and cannot predict about one person's risk (route entry bio-m5-g03).

teaching.task: What can data pooled from huge numbers of people (or animals) show that one family or one hospital can't, and how far can we trust what it shows?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why scale helps (chance swamps small effects in small samples, 2); why the sickle map is a puzzle (selection should remove a harmful allele, 3); why three streams are needed (each misses something, 4); why carriers are favoured (no anaemia, less severe malaria, so more children, 5); why a match is not proof (coincidence; founders, 6); why diversity matters (more alleles, more chance some resist a new disease, 7); why shared variants mean relatedness (inherited from common ancestors, 8). Visible case: one map, one devil tray pair, one bar chart. Video advantage: the simulation settles live; the malaria layer slides over the allele map; founder beads carry an allele to an island; a disease passes along two trays. Thinking opportunities: two unseen data items with every value and demand on screen. Reading load: one board at a time; the scene 8 frame is the busiest and builds one element per cue.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Opens on the hook (hook (half a million volunteers)), then works through why scale matters, the sickle cell puzzle, three kinds of evidence, the malaria overlay, a match isn't proof and the remaining scenes in order, with each reasoning stage shown on its own cue; ends with the unseen attempt (10 second countdown), brief feedback, the decision rule or board, and the key notes.
teaching.openingDecision: UK Biobank is a shared research project that began recruiting in 2006. Half a million volunteers in Britain, aged 40 to 69, gave blood samples and agreed to link their health records. So what can data from half a million people show that one family, or one hospital, never could? And how far can we trust it?
teaching.understandingCheck: 11a is a data table (example data, labelled) of a red blood cell variant's frequency and malaria level in six regions, one of them an island that breaks the trend: it tests describing a trend, naming a relationship as a suggestion, and giving a rival explanation. 11c is conservation data (example data) for a mainland and an island wallaby population: it tests reading diversity, inferring population history and naming a management use, with the diversity trap. Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; each card stays on screen during and after the countdown. Each feedback is brief (about 25 s): answer, key reason, one crossed-out classic mistake. No mark-allocation talk.
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (2017, BIO12-12, programme/syllabus/bio-2017-y12.json, B5-IQ5-03 to B5-IQ5-06, p 50): "investigate the use of data analysis from a large-scale collaborative project to identify trends, patterns and relationships, for example: (ACSBL064, ACSBL073)" with the examples "the use of population genetics data in conservation management", "population genetics studies used to determine the inheritance of a disease or disorder" and "population genetics relating to human evolution". The two spaces before "for example" are in the official DOCX extraction (pack note). Route action B-collaborative-data. The parent line is marked as a depth-study or practical opportunity; this video supplies the concepts and two analysis tasks, not a student investigation. Update the ledger row for B-collaborative-data when this design passes review.

design.visualSystem: Three boards, one at a time. (1) The data board (scenes 1, 2, 9): a coded grid of many small sample-tube chips that pools into one data bar; SampleBounce from B11 (seeded rng) reused to show a small study's estimate bouncing and a large study's estimate settling. (2) The map board (scenes 3 to 6, attempt 1): a coded world outline (simplified public-domain outline, for example Natural Earth 110 m, drawn as a single stroke; no painted map), with region shading for allele frequency drawn from banded values (legend with written bands, never colour only), a second overlay layer for malaria, and evidence cards (pedigree, DNA strip, frequency) docked at the side. (3) The population board (scenes 7, 8): allele-bead trays (B11's bead look) for diversity, and a coded bar chart and a simple coded similarity tree for the 1000 Genomes pattern. Individuals are never drawn as people: pedigree symbols, tube chips or beads only. Amber is the emphasis colour only.
design.transitionPlan: The data board (sample tubes pooling into one bar and the small-against-large simulation) opens the lesson and gives way to the map board for scenes 3 to 6, where the allele map, the evidence cards and the malaria overlay build on one outline; the population board takes over for scenes 7 and 8 and the data board returns for scene 9; each attempt card clears the board and its feedback shrinks the card to a strip and builds the model answer one point at a time; the next chip slides in; scene crossfade with settle.

scenes.teachingReason: Why scale matters: A project like this is called a large-scale collaborative project: many researchers and sites pool their data.
scenes.narrationCue: many researchers and sites pool their data / only nudge risk a little / In a small study / hundreds of thousands / inference / never certain
scenes.motionPurpose: On "only nudge risk a little" two bars appear, "carriers" and "non-carriers", differing by a sliver (illustrative; tag "a small real difference"). On "In a small study" B11's SampleBounce runs with n = 200: repeated estimates of the difference scatter widely, some below zero (computed with seeded rng; as the first dots land the tag "each dot: one small study's result" writes on, then "200 people: chance swamps it").
scenes.onScreenChange: on "many researchers and sites pool their data" five site badges each send a stream of chips into one central bar; the term writes on with the gloss "many groups pooling data". On "only nudge risk a little" two bars appear, "carriers" and "non-carriers", differing by a sliver (illustrative; tag "a small real difference"). On "hundreds of thousands" the same simulation reruns with n = 200,000 and the dots cluster tightly above zero (tags "each dot: one big study's result" and "200,000 people: the real difference shows"). scenes.teachingReason: The sickle cell puzzle: Pooling data isn't new.

On "should become rare" a small coded line graph draws a frequency falling towards zero over generations (tag "expected: selection removes it"; grey tag "Year 11: natural selection").
scenes.onScreenChange: the map board. m6-red-cells-normal-sickle-v1.png sits small at the upper left (tag "two copies: sickle cell anaemia"). On "combined into one map" many small survey dots drop onto the coded world outline and merge into shaded regions (WorldShade, banded legend written: "under 1%", "1 to 5%", "5 to 10%", "over 10%" of allele copies; source tag "redrawn from Piel et al. 2010, bands simplified"; shading drawn from the published figure, not by eye). On "large parts of Africa" the African bands brighten; on "Mediterranean, the Middle East and India" small shaded patches pulse in turn. scenes.visualReference: three EvidenceCards dock at the right of the map in turn.

scenes.teachingReason: Protecting a threatened species: The same kind of data helps protect threatened species.
scenes.narrationCue: contagious facial cancer / very little genetic diversity / past population crashes / helps against a new disease / pair devils that are less related / doesn't guarantee survival
scenes.motionPurpose: The painted devil plate (m5x-tasmanian-devil-v1.png, new) enters at the left with a small coded map chip of Tasmania. On "contagious facial cancer" a grey tag writes on: "devil facial tumour disease, first seen 1996".
scenes.onScreenChange: the population board. The painted devil plate (m5x-tasmanian-devil-v1.png, new) enters at the left with a small coded map chip of Tasmania. On "very little genetic diversity" two DiversityTrays draw side by side, each a row of five markers: "a diverse population" with many bead colours per marker, "devils" with one or two colours per marker (illustrative; grey tag "illustrative pattern, not measured values"). scenes.visualReference: on "1000 Genomes Project" a coded title card writes on with "2,504 people, 26 populations" (source tag "1000 Genomes Project, 2015"); 26 small region dots light on a faint world outline.

scenes.narrationCue: 1000 Genomes Project / share more variants / the most variation / most common variants found elsewhere / each group that left was a small set of founders / the reference genome / four to five million places
scenes.motionPurpose: On "share more variants" two pairs of variant strips compare: a pair sharing many amber ticks (tag "more shared: more recent common ancestors") and a pair sharing few. On "the most variation" VariantBars draw: five continental-group bars of variant sites per genome, the African-ancestry bar tallest (values from the phase 3 paper; tag "variant sites per genome").
scenes.onScreenChange: on "1000 Genomes Project" a coded title card writes on with "2,504 people, 26 populations" (source tag "1000 Genomes Project, 2015"); 26 small region dots light on a faint world outline.
